questions.question: Riya's school has 600 students. She writes all 600 names on identical slips, mixes them in a box, and pulls out 50 slips without looking. Which name best fits her sampling method?
options: A random sample, since every student had the same chance of being drawn
A convenience sample, since the slips were sitting right there in the box
A voluntary sample, since the students let their names go into the box
A systematic sample, since she drew the slips one right after another
questions.explain: Random means every member of the population has an equal chance of being chosen, which is exactly what mixing 600 slips and drawing blind does; a sample is not random just because it was easy to take or because people agreed to be in it.

questions.question: A Kelowna radio station asks listeners to phone in and say whether the city should build a new skate park. 84 people call and 71 of them say yes. Why is this sample likely to be biased?
options: It is not biased, since every listener was free to phone in
Only listeners with strong feelings bother to phone in
It is biased only because 84 callers is fewer than 100 people
It is not biased, since the callers picked themselves
questions.explain: This is a voluntary-response sample: the callers choose themselves, so people with strong opinions are over-represented. Letting people choose themselves does not make a sample fair, and the size of the sample is not the real problem here.

questions.question: A Grade 9 class has 12 students who bus to school, 8 who walk, and 5 who bike, for 25 students in total. The teacher randomly picks 3 bus riders, 2 walkers, and 1 biker to interview. Which name fits her method?
options: Convenience, since she used the groups already sitting together
Voluntary, since students in each travel group agreed to talk
Stratified, since each travel group is sampled separately
Systematic, since she counted off students in a fixed pattern
questions.explain: Stratified sampling splits the population into groups (strata) and takes a random sample from each group, so every group is represented. Counting off at a fixed interval would be systematic, and grabbing whoever is nearby would be convenience.

questions.question: Before school, Jai stands at the north door and asks the first 10 students who walk in whether they like the new bell schedule. How should his sample be described?
options: It is a random sample, since Jai could not know who would arrive first
It is a random sample, since ten students is a fair-sized group
It is a voluntary sample, since the students agreed to answer him
It is a convenience sample, since he asked whoever was easy to ask
questions.explain: Asking whoever happens to be closest is a convenience sample. Students who use other doors or arrive later have no chance of being picked, so 'I could not predict who walks in' does not make it random.

questions.question: A school of 800 students wants to know how much time students spend on homework each night. Which plan gives the least biased sample of 80 students?
options: Number all 800 students and let a computer pick 80
Ask 80 students studying in the library after school
Put up a sign-up sheet and take the first 80 to sign
Ask the 80 students named on the school honour roll
questions.explain: Only numbering the whole population and picking at random gives every student an equal chance. Library students and honour-roll students likely do more homework, and a sign-up sheet only captures students who choose to answer.

questions.question: A secondary school has 400 Grade 8s, 300 Grade 9s, 200 Grade 10s and 100 seniors, for 1000 students. Student council wants a sample of 100 whose opinions on a new lunch menu reflect the whole school. Which plan does that best?
options: Take 100 students at random from the Grade 8 hallway
Randomly pick 40 Grade 8s, 30 Nines, 20 Tens, 10 seniors
Ask the first 100 students who comment on the school app
Ask 25 students from each of the four grade groups, evenly
questions.explain: A stratified sample takes each grade in proportion to its size, so 40, 30, 20 and 10 match the 400, 300, 200 and 100 in the school. Taking 25 from every grade over-weights the small senior group, and app comments come only from volunteers.

questions.question: A recreation centre has 1000 members and wants to survey 50 of them about pool hours. Which plan is a systematic sample?
options: Survey the first 50 members who arrive Saturday morning
Survey the 50 members who drop a note in the comment box
Survey every 20th name on the alphabetical member list
Draw 50 member numbers out of a hat after mixing well
questions.explain: Systematic sampling means moving down a list at a fixed interval, such as every 20th name. Drawing numbers from a hat is random, and taking whoever shows up first is convenience, not systematic.

questions.question: Mei wants the mean weekly amount that Grade 9s at her school spend on transit. She surveys 30 students waiting at the bus stop outside the school. Which statement describes her sample best?
options: It is random, because Mei cannot know who will be waiting there
It is unbiased, because all 30 students answered by choice
It is biased, because 30 students is too few to mean anything
It is biased, because students who never bus cannot be picked
questions.explain: A sample is biased when part of the population has no chance of being selected, and walkers, bikers and drivers are shut out here, which pushes the mean transit cost up. Not being able to predict who is standing there does not make it random.

questions.question: A town of 5000 residents is deciding whether to extend a bike lane. A councillor surveys 120 people at the Saturday farmers market; 90 percent say yes. The council then reports that 90 percent of residents support the plan. Why is that report misleading?
options: Market visitors likely walk or cycle more, so support looks too high
The shoppers answered on their own, so the survey carries no bias
The percent should come from the median of the answers, not a count
The 120 shoppers count as random, so the only worry is the small size
questions.explain: Two steps: the market crowd is a convenience sample, and it leans toward people who already walk or cycle, so the 90 percent is too high for the whole town. Being unable to predict who is at the market does not make the sample random.

questions.question: A school newspaper posts an online poll asking if the dance should move to Friday; 210 of the 950 students answer and 180 say yes. The editor could instead phone 60 students picked at random from the full student list. Which result should the editor trust more?
options: The poll of 210, because far more students took part in it
The 60 random calls, because every student had an equal chance
The poll of 210, because students answered it of their own choice
The 60 random calls, because phoned answers are more honest
questions.explain: A large voluntary-response sample is still biased, because only students who care enough to click are counted; a smaller random sample represents all 950 students because each one had an equal chance of being called.

questions.question: Owen must estimate the mean amount Grade 9s spend on lunch. He asks the 15 students standing in the food-truck line at 12:05 and gets a mean of $9.40, but the true mean for all Grade 9s is $6.10. What best explains the gap?
options: His 15 students were random, so the gap is just ordinary chance
He should have used the median, which is always nearer the truth
Food-truck buyers spend more than students who bring lunch
The students answered willingly, so his sample cannot be biased
questions.explain: The food-truck line is a convenience sample of exactly the students who spend money, so the mean comes out too high. A convenience sample is not random, and switching to the median would not repair a sample that leaves out home-lunch students.

questions.question: A community centre wants to know how its 1200 members feel about opening an hour earlier. A staff member plans to ask the 40 members in the 7 a.m. fitness class. Which change would best remove the bias?
options: Ask the first 40 members through the door, which is random
Ask 40 members who volunteer to fill a form at the desk
Ask 80 members of the 7 a.m. class, to double the sample
Ask 40 members chosen at random from the full member list
questions.explain: Members already at the centre at 7 a.m. obviously favour early hours, so the fix must give every one of the 1200 members a chance, which only random selection from the full list does. Doubling a biased sample or grabbing whoever walks in first keeps the same bias.
